The workflow combines controlled surrogate extrapolation, targeted charge-transfer-region interpolation, and independent DFT verification to obtain polaron migration pathways, emphasizing reproducible barriers and full-band force convergence.

items.title: Excitation Spectra of the Frustrated Spin-1/2 $J_1$-$J_2$ Model via Dual Spin-Sector Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
items.summary: Finding excited states and excitation gaps in frustrated spin systems using Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQE) is complicated by state-ordering inversions. In the frustrated spin-1/2 $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model, standard single-sector algorithms like Variational Quantum Deflation (VQD) in $S_z=0$ fail when $J_2/J_1 < 0.25$. In this regime, the lowest-lying excitation in $S_z=0$ is a Triplet ($S=1$), which lies below the Excited Singlet ($S=0$). Standard deflation projects out the ground singlet and converges onto the Triplet state, misidentifying it as the Excited Singlet. Here, this work presents a Dual Spin-Sector VQE framework that resolves these state-ordering inversions applied to frustrated $J_1-J_2$ models on 1D spin chains and 2D rectangular lattices. Firstly, by optimizing the ground Triplet state in the $S_z=1$ sector (where singlet states cannot exist), mapping it into $S_z=0$ via the total spin-lowering operator $S^- = \sum_i S_i^-$, and evaluating a dual-sector penalty cost function, the Excited Singlet ($E_S$) is isolated without variational ambiguity. Numerical state-vector simulations confirm exact convergence to machine precision with unit overlap fidelity. The method captures key physical features, including the gapless phase, the gapless-gapped critical point at $J_2/J_1 \approx 0.2411$, the Majumdar-Ghosh dimer point ($J_2/J_1 = 0.50$), and the 2D non-magnetic frustrated regime ($J_2/J_1 \approx 0.40 - 0.60$). Finite-shot sampling simulations and gate-scaling analytics up to $N=100$ qubits demonstrate the resource efficiency and shot resilience of the algorithm for near-term quantum execution.

items.title: Molecular Precursor Chemistry Shapes Early-Stage Reaction Pathways in Nitrogen-Doped Carbon Nanotube Synthesis
items.summary: The structural characteristics of carbon nanotubes are usually discussed in terms of processes occurring during nanotube nucleation and subsequent growth from an already formed catalyst nanoparticle. Here, we show that their structural trajectory can begin much earlier, within the first nanoseconds of precursor decomposition and catalyst formation. We combine experiment and reactive molecular dynamics to compare nitrogen-free CNT synthesis with two closely related aromatic nitrogen precursors, pyridine and pyrazine, containing one and two nitrogen atoms per molecule, respectively. Experimentally, both nitrogen-containing precursors promote bamboo-like CNT formation and produce substantially more structurally disordered CNTs than the nitrogen-free reference. Notably, nitrogen incorporation does not scale simply with the amount of nitrogen supplied, demonstrating a strong contribution from precursor chemistry. Reactive molecular dynamics reveals that nitrogen-containing precursors significantly modify local Fe-carbon and Fe-SiO2 interactions during catalyst evolution, while pyridine and pyrazine exhibit distinct decomposition pathways, with pyrazine showing significantly greater decomposition within the simulated timescale. These results demonstrate that precursor chemistry influences the local chemical environment and early catalyst evolution, highlighting its potential role in the initial stages of CNT growth.

items.title: Multicomponent Magnetic Domain Walls in Rhombohedral Graphene
items.summary: Spatial textures of magnetic order, such as domain walls and skyrmions, are fundamental objects in magnetism. In rhombohedral multilayer graphene, magnetic order involves spin and valley degrees of freedom, opening the possibility of qualitatively new spatial textures. Here, we explore this possibility through a microscopic study of a one-dimensional domain wall in the valley-imbalanced quarter-metal phase of rhombohedral graphene. We uncover two different classes of domain walls. One resembles a conventional magnetic domain wall, locally rotating between the two bulk states, whereas the other is intrinsically multicomponent and explores states that are not occupied in either bulk domain. Which texture is realized is controlled by the competition between intervalley Hund's coupling and spin-orbit coupling, and we identify experimental signatures to distinguish them. For a superconducting junction formed across the wall, we further show that the superconducting phase difference couples directly to the intervalley-coherent phase of the texture, allowing precession of this internal phase to generate a voltage. This mechanism provides an explanation for the resistive domain walls recently observed in chiral superconductors [arXiv2605.13303] and predicts accompanying magnetization oscillations that could be detected using GHz-frequency AC probes. Our theory establish a microscopic connection between multicomponent magnetic textures, their internal dynamics, and superconducting transport.

items.title: Lower bounds on entropy production from dynamical correlation functions
items.summary: Entropy production is a key property in stochastic thermodynamics. For partially observed and coarse-grained systems, its inference is challenging and typically rests on proven lower bounds. We derive two versions of such bounds based on the asymmetry of experimentally accessible two-time correlation functions of coarse-grained state observables. For non-equilibrium steady states, the bound is valid for arbitrary correlation lag. For time-dependent processes, it requires the limit of vanishing lag. These bounds hold true for any system that follows either a Markovian dynamics or a coupled set of overdamped Langevin equations on some underlying, unobservable level of description. We illustrate the bounds for both types of dynamics and discuss their optimization and potential tightness.

items.title: Self-phoresis on a one-dimensional periodic domain
items.summary: We study the spontaneous motion and collective dynamics of self-phoretic particles on a one-dimensional periodic domain. The particles act as localized chemical sources (of a particle-dependent strength) of a field and the particles themselves respond to the gradients of the field they generate (with a particle-dependent phoretic mobility). The chemical field itself diffuses and evaporates. For a single particle, we derive the exact threshold for spontaneous propulsion and establish the emergence of stable constant-velocity states near onset through a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation. We then consider an active source coupled to a non-emitting tracer and determine the conditions for slipping and stable phase-locked motion. For two mutually coupled sources, the stationary antipodal configuration can lose stability through either a pitchfork or a Hopf bifurcation, depending on the relative source strengths and phoretic mobilities. We determine the competing instability thresholds and compare them with direct numerical simulations of the coupled particle-field equations. Beyond onset, the resulting translating and oscillatory states provide qualitative counterparts to modes of motion observed experimentally for camphor disks in annular water channels. These results connect the onset of individual propulsion, tracer entrainment, and collective motion within a common analytically tractable framework.

items.title: Information Entropy as a Sensitive Diagnostic of Relaxation Dynamics in a Quasiperiodic Mott Insulator
items.summary: We study the nonequilibrium dynamics of a bosonic Mott insulator following a sudden quench from a periodic to a quasiperiodic lattice. Using ab initio multiconfigurational (MCTDHB) continuum many-body dynamics, we characterize the evolution through momentum distributions, fragmenta- tion, correlation functions, and information entropy. We find that melting of Mott correlations does not necessarily imply relaxation of the many-body state. In the weakly interacting regime, the initial Mott-like correlation undergo recurrent melting and partial recovery, while the information entropy displays large, intermittent fluctuations within the simulated time window. In contrast, a strongly interacting and fully fragmented Mott insulator retains its characteristic Mott correla- tions, up to partial distortions, while the many-body information entropy approaches a well-defined stationary regime plateau with comparatively small fluctuations. These results indicate that Mott- correlation dynamics and many-body relaxation can be dissociated in this finite system and support the use of information entropy, evaluated in the multiconfigurational representation, as a sensitive complementary diagnostic of nonequilibrium relaxation.

items.title: peaks: a Python package for analysis of angle-resolved photoemission and related spectroscopies
items.summary: The electronic band structure, describing the motion and interactions of electrons in materials, dictates the electrical, optical, and thermodynamic properties of solids. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) provides a direct experimental probe of such electronic band structures, and so is widely employed in the study of functional, quantum, and 2D materials. \texttt{peaks} (\textbf{P}ython \textbf{E}lectron spectroscopy \textbf{A}nalysis by \textbf{K}ing group @ \textbf{S}t Andrews) provides a Python package for advanced data analysis of ARPES and related spectroscopic data. It facilitates the fast visualisation and analysis of multi-dimensional datasets, allows for the complex data hierarchy typical to ARPES experiments, and supports lazy data loading and parallel processing, reflecting the ever-increasing data volumes used in ARPES. It is designed to be run in an interactive notebook environment, with extensive inline and pop-out GUI support for data visualisation.

items.title: Quantum Ising transition on the Cayley tree: boundary criticality, universality, and an effective Bethe line
items.summary: We investigate quantum criticality in the transverse-field Ising model on finite Cayley trees and demonstrate that their extensive boundary fundamentally changes the nature of the quantum phase transition compared with the infinite, boundary-free Bethe lattice. Using tree tensor-network simulations for systems with up to $N=12286$ sites, we identify a boundary-driven continuous transition at $h_x^c\approx1.76$, distinct from the mean-field Bethe-lattice transition at $h_x^c\approx2.23$. We characterize this transition through finite-size scaling of the magnetization and magnetic susceptibility and extract a consistent set of critical exponents. By introducing next-nearest-neighbor interactions, we demonstrate the robustness of the extracted critical exponents, providing numerical argument for the Ising boundary universality class on the Cayley tree. Furthermore, we show that the physics of the boundary-free Bethe lattice can be efficiently recovered on a finite Cayley tree by fine-tuning a local boundary field. The resulting \textit{effective Bethe line}, whose existence is tied to the mean-field nature of the bulk transition, effectively screens the extensive boundary and restores both the critical point and the mean-field critical scaling of the infinite Bethe lattice.

items.title: Engineering Ferroelectric Phases in BaTiO$_3$ Films via Buffer-Layer Induced Misfit Strain Reversal
items.summary: Controlling ferroelectric phase symmetry through strain engineering is crucial for tailoring polarization topology and functional properties in oxide-based devices. Here, we show that a thin conductive buffer layer can override substrate-induced strain in BaTiO$_3$ (BTO) films on MgO. Although the lattice parameter of MgO(001) would be expected to induce tensile misfit strain, in 500~nm BaTiO$_3$ films the thermal-expansion mismatch dominates, resulting in effective compressive stress upon cooling. Inserting a 50-nm La$_{0.67}$Sr$_{0.33}$MnO$_3$ (LSMO) buffer layer reverses the effective strain state from compressive to tensile. Using temperature-dependent polarized Raman spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and piezoresponse force microscopy, we reveal an unconventional phase sequence upon cooling: paraelectric $\rightarrow$ orthorhombic ($\textit{aa}$-phase, $\sim$407 K) $\rightarrow$ monoclinic ($\textit{r}$-phase, $\sim$300-345 K), characterized in-plane and tilted polarization components. The LSMO layer not only serves as a bottom electrode but also modifies the strain state, while interfacial charge redistribution induces a built-in electric field, evidenced by self-polarization and asymmetric PFM hysteresis. These findings highlight the critical role of conductive buffer layers in controlling ferroelectric symmetry and enabling oxide heterostructures with tailored polarization textures for low-power spintronics, tunable microwave devices, and neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Transport Determines Spectral Distance in Mesoscopic Thermodynamics
items.summary: We derive a distance between thermodynamic states from a positive Hermitian transport tensor within a mesoscopic canonical model. An exact first-order factorization of the evolution generator gives a commutator norm and the metric $G=2g^{-1}$, where $g$ denotes the symmetric transport tensor. Gradients of the antisymmetric tensor can change the evolution, but they leave this distance unchanged. The construction allows coordinate-dependent coefficients. For constant Onsager coefficients, a Clifford representation gives the same metric. In a two-channel thermoelectric system, the ratio of normalized principal distances is $\sqrt{1+ZT}+\sqrt{ZT}$. Transport coupling thus fixes the anisotropy of this metric. The construction requires neither an independent metric nor a physical spin variable.

items.title: Impact of shear and dilational membrane viscosities on capsule shape and dynamics under shear flow: a theoretical study
items.summary: In artificial (micro)capsules or cells such as red blood cells for example, the two-dimensional (2D) rheology of the membrane (or the shell) is viscoelastic and not only elastic. The deformation and inclination of such a capsule are theoretically studied under shear and extensional flows. The membrane mechanics is described by the Kelvin-Voigt model: the 2D dissipation with the Boussinesq-Scriven law associated to specific dilational and shear Boussinesq numbers $Bq_d$ and $Bq_d$ respectively while the elastic constitutive law is either Hookean, strain-softening (neoHookean) or strain-hardening (Skalak). The dynamics depends on the elastic capillary number $Ca$, the Poisson ratio (or $C$ in Skalak law), the viscosity ratio $λ$, the nonlinearities included in the constitutive law and both boussinesq numbers. Three dynamics are identified in the limit of weak deformations: a tank-treading motion in the limit of small elastic capillary number with a characteristic time depending on $λ$, $Bq_s$ and $Bq_d$, an oscillation without any elasticity and a damped oscillation leading to a tank-treading motion in the limit of large Boussinesq numbers. In all cases, both shear and dilational 2D dissipations contribute differently leading to non-trivial results. In the case of a Skalak law with $C=1$, $Bq=Bq_s=Bq_d$ and $Bq>>λ$, the deformations in the limits $Ca >1$ determined in the seminal work of \cite{barthes1985role} are recovered.

items.title: Emergent Spinorial Structure in Mesoscopic Irreversible Thermodynamics
items.summary: We reconstruct a geometry of thermodynamic coordinates from transport coefficients within a mesoscopic canonical model. Self-adjoint flux observables determine a compatible evolution generator containing symmetric and antisymmetric transport coefficients. When the Hermitian transport tensor is positive, an exact graded first-order factorization reproduces this generator on its scalar sector. Its commutators define a spectral distance whose metric depends only on the symmetric tensor. Gradients of the antisymmetric tensor can change the evolution while leaving the metric unchanged. The construction allows coordinate-dependent coefficients. In the constant Onsager regime, a Clifford representation gives the same distance and an algebra fixed by the transport matrix. Published transport data for a $\mathrm{Bi_2Te_3}$ film give a principal-distance ratio of approximately $2.12$ in normalized coordinates at $ZT\simeq0.68$. We also examine a separate quadratic entropy-production observable and distinguish its discrete spectrum from the spectrum of the evolution generator. The spinorial representation adds no physical spin degrees of freedom.

items.title: Dynamics of ring polymer melts: Memory function approach
items.summary: We investigated the static and dynamic properties of a Rouse ring polymer modified by introducing an effective, spherically symmetric, attractive potential of entropic nature and a memory function describing the effect of dynamic entanglement. Renormalized Rouse formalism is used to approximate the time dependence of the memory matrix. The results obtained are in good agreement with existing experimental data and the results of computer simulations of ring polymer ring with , , where N_e is the number of Kuhn segments in linear polymer melts between neighboring entanglements and , the number of Kuhn segments. For large molecular weights, a refined self-consistent approximation is proposed to describe the time dependence of the memory function. It is shown that this approximation allows us to describe an exponential decrease in the self-diffusion coefficient with molecular weight of the rings, i.e., the effect of dynamic localization.

items.title: 1/f frequency-noise reduction in nanomechanical resonators by dissipation dilution
items.summary: The frequency noise of a resonant nanomechanical sensor is well understood down to its thermomechanical limit, but the longest useful averaging time is set by a flicker, or $1/f$, frequency-noise floor whose origin has remained unknown. We show that this floor is the thermal noise of the tension. By the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the tension of a resonator with fixed ends fluctuates by an amount set by the loss angle of its material; for structural damping, these fluctuations produce $1/f$ frequency noise with a flicker coefficient $h_{-1}=E k_{\mathrm{B}} T/(2πVσ_0^2 Q_{\mathrm{el}})$, with $Q_{\mathrm{el}}$ the intrinsic loss under elongation, that contains no free parameter and is diluted by the tensile stress $σ_0$ in the same way as damping is in dissipation dilution. Silicon nitride strings and membranes from 30 to 340~nm thickness follow the predicted volume scaling, the predicted $σ_0^{-2}$ dilution across resonators and within stress-engineered strings, and the predicted thickness dependence, which places noise-active two-level systems in the volume and at the surfaces of the resonators, all at the absolute level set by the independently measured intrinsic loss. The same relation accounts for published data between 78 and 296~K; below 78~K, the loss measured at the resonance no longer represents the loss probed by the noise, marking the limit of the structural-damping assumption. Dissipation dilution therefore lowers the $1/f$ floor, and the longest useful integration time of a resonant sensor is set by its prestress, volume, temperature, and intrinsic loss angle.

items.title: Influence-solvability: a systematic theory of $(1+1)D$ solvability and its application to brickwork circuits
items.summary: `Solvable' circuits, such as dual unitaries and its generalisations, have arisen as paradigmatic examples of tractable chaotic non-equilibrium dynamics, both in classical and quantum systems. However, while increasingly complicated sufficient conditions have been proposed, a systematic theory classifying and understanding general features of Solvable circuits is missing. In this work we develop such a theory by deriving the most general local necessary and sufficient conditions under which a $(1+1)D$ circuit is Solvable. Concretely, we define a circuit to be \emph{influence-solvable} if its influence matrix, representing the `bath' generated by its own evolution, is given by a uniform MPS with finite bond-dimension $χ$. This property allows for efficient computation of subsystem dynamics and essentially contains all known examples of Solvable circuits. The set of necessary and sufficient local conditions follows from a new version of the fundamental theorem of MPS for open boundary conditions. Next, we apply our theory to brickwork circuits with $χ=1$ influence-solvability and perform a systematic classification of classical brickwork circuits with local dimension up to $d=3$ and quantum brickwork circuits with $d=2$. Our search reveals new Solvable circuits that are not captured by known conditions.

items.title: Thermal Signatures of the Slater-Mott Crossover in the Hubbard Model: From Double Occupancy to Antiferromagnetic Correlation Length
items.summary: The interaction-driven crossover from a Slater insulator to a Mott insulator in the Néel-ordered ground state of the Hubbard model is a fundamental paradigm of strongly correlated electrons, yet its quantitative characterization has remained elusive. Here we establish a clear and experimentally accessible thermal criterion for this crossover via the sign change of the temperature derivative of double occupancy, $(\partial D/\partial T)_U$, near zero temperature. In the Slater regime, $(\partial D/\partial T)_U>0$ reflects the major role of charge fluctuations; in the Mott regime, the anomalous $(\partial D/\partial T)_U<0$, a manifestation of the Pomeranchuk effect, signals the dominance of low-energy spin superexchange physics. Using exact diagonalization and {\it numerically exact} quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that this criterion determines the crossover boundary at $U_{\rm cross}/t=4.0(2)$ for the half-filled two-dimensional Hubbard model. Furthermore, we obtain a consistent boundary independently from the maximum in the antiferromagnetic correlation length, which also arises from the superexchange physics. These two thermal signatures are theoretically unified through the local minimum of thermal entropy versus interaction $U$ at low temperatures. Our results offer a direct, measurable, and physically intuitive framework to identify the Slater-Mott crossover in optical lattice experiments.

items.title: Pressure-induced decoupling of the pseudogap and superconductivity in a bilayer cuprate
items.summary: The physical origin of the pseudogap in cuprate superconductors, whether a precursor to superconductivity or a distinct intertwined order, remains an open question. Although hydrostatic pressure provides a clean tuning parameter, probing the relevant energy scales under compression has remained experimentally elusive. Here, we employ ultrafast optical spectroscopy to track the non-equilibrium quasiparticle dynamics of slightly underdoped Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+δ}$ up to 37 GPa. By disentangling the pseudogap and superconducting relaxation channels in the time domain, we uncover a contrasting pressure evolution: despite an increase in carrier density, the pseudogap thermal onset (T$^*$) rises monotonically, whereas its energy gap ($Δ_{PG}$) is continuously suppressed. Conversely, the critical temperature (T$_C$) and the superconducting gap ($Δ_{SC}$) exhibit a synchronized dome-like trajectory. The effective coupling ratio 2$Δ_{SC}$/k$_B$T$_C$ collapses abruptly from ~10 toward the weak-coupling d-wave limit, signifying a crossover from a phase-fluctuating two-dimensional regime to a globally coherent three-dimensional state. Upon compression to 37 GPa, the superconducting condensate is completely quenched into an insulating-like state, yet the pseudogap persists. The extended phase diagram reveals an unambiguous decoupling between the pseudogap and superconductivity, imposing stringent constraints on microscopic theories of high-temperature superconductivity.

items.title: Colloid-Colloid Interactions Impact Network Morphology of Confined Colloidal Drying Patterns
items.summary: Colloidal suspensions that are confined between two closely spaced plates and left to evaporate slowly form maze-like labyrinth patterns in the final stage of evaporation. The fingers in these patterns form bifurcations and occasionally loops, which we may quantify with a skeletonization method. We compare drying patterns formed with two different salt concentrations in the droplet which changes the screening length and therefore the effective colloid interactions. We find that the junctions generally follow Murray's law for optimal transport networks, and that the typical bifurcation angles peak around 53. Screened droplets additionally show more loopy networks, and is characterized by bands of transversal fingers before merging into a central non-fingering colloidal aggregate. Our observations suggest that colloid-colloid interactions can strongly influence the large-scale topology of the pattern while leaving the local geometry of the individual fingers unchanged.

items.title: Reformulating Pfaffian Quantum Monte Carlo with the Hybrid Monte Carlo formalism
items.summary: Pfaffian quantum Monte Carlo extends auxiliary field methods to anomalous fermionic Hamiltonians, opening access to pairing systems and Hubbard--Stratonovich decompositions that are unavailable in determinant formulations. We show that this flexibility can be combined with the global updates of Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC), leading to an algorithm scaling as $\mathcal{O}(N_τL^3)$, similar to its determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) counterpart without pseudofermions. The central observation is that the molecular dynamics force depends only on the magnitude of the Pfaffian weight, which admits a determinant representation and leads to a simplified force expression. This construction also yields unequal-time Majorana correlators at essentially no additional cost. We demonstrate the method for the interacting Kitaev chain using the imaginary and symmetric Majorana hopping channel. The resulting noncommuting auxiliary-field bond operators are treated through an even-odd decomposition. Their block structure permits an analytic reduction to a sparse effective interaction matrix of bandwidth two and allows explicit force expressions. Results agree with exact diagonalization and resolve low-energy modes localized at opposite boundaries, together with their increasing overlap near the topological transition of the non-interacting system. These findings establish HMC as an efficient sampling framework for Pfaffian auxiliary-field simulations.

items.title: Destructive Interference of a Charge Density Wave in the Skyrmion Magnet GdRu2Si2
items.summary: In skyrmion magnets, charge density waves induce higher-order exchange interactions that can select multi-Q ground states. Using resonant X-ray scattering and neutron diffraction, we measure temperature-dependent spin-charge coupling in GdRu2Si2. A minimal Landau model with one critical exponent and two ordering temperatures reproduces all six observed order parameters. Spin-density wave components of the multi-Q ground state drive charge ordering, but the onset of a magnetic helix suppresses it via destructive interference.

items.title: Domain-wall-to-domain interconversion in a polar conducting oxide
items.summary: Domain walls in ferroic crystals are topological defects with a symmetry distinct from the domain interior, allowing them to display functionalities that are otherwise forbidden in the host material. Despite their unique properties, domain walls are strictly confined to two-dimensional interfaces, which hinders unveiling their true nature and limits their applicability. Here, we demonstrate reversible dimensionality control by expanding nanoscale domain walls into three-dimensional functional regions in polar epitaxial tungsten trioxide ($\text{WO}_3$). This domain-wall-to-domain interconversion is enabled by the conducting, non-polar domain walls adopting the parent-phase structure. An alternating electric field applied through a scanning probe tip induces localized heating, which expands this domain-wall phase into the adjacent polar domains. This approach enables reversible spatial control to switch between mutually exclusive properties of domains (polarity) and domain walls (conductivity), offering a new paradigm for reconfigurable oxide electronics.

items.title: Confinement-deconfinement transitions in the dimer-loop models on two-dimensional non-bipartite lattices
items.summary: Recent work [Kundu, Damle, Phys. Rev. X 15, 011018 (2025)] has demonstrated that a class of $S=1$ kagome lattice antiferromagnets with competing anisotropies can exhibit unusual low-temperature behavior that is best described in terms of the statistical mechanics of an interesting interpolation between the fully-packed dimer model and the fully-packed loop model on the bipartite honeycomb lattice. On this and other bipartite lattices in two and three dimension, such fully-packed dimer-loop models generically have two distinct power-law correlated Coulomb phases, both of which admit a low-energy description in terms of a fluctuating divergence-free polarization vector field [Phys. Rev. X 15, 011018 (2025); arXiv:2510.11607]. The transition between these phases corresponds to a confinement transition for the $Z_2$ part of the corresponding $U(1)$ flux [Phys. Rev. X 15, 011018 (2025); arXiv:2510.11607]. Here we demonstrate that a variant of such a topological confinement transition can also exist in dimer-loop models on non-bipartite lattices such as the kagome and triangular lattices although the low-energy description does not feature any conserved $U(1)$ flux. In these non-bipartite dimer-loop models, both phases are short-range correlated liquids, and the topological distinction between them is in terms of a $Z_2$-valued winding number instead of the flux of a divergence-free polarization field. In spite of this key difference, this transition appears to be in the same Ising universality class as the analogous transition of the bipartite dimer-loop models. These kagome and triangular lattice dimer-loop models correspond respectively to the low-energy limit of a class of $S=1$ antiferromagnets with competing anisotropies on the ruby lattice comprising a corner-sharing arrangement of fully-frustrated squares and a lattice of corner-sharing fully-frustrated hexagons.

items.title: Topological Chiral Superconductivity from Doping Correlated Charge Transfer Insulator with Orbital Magnetism
items.summary: Topological chiral superconductivity has been extensively studied from the perspective of electronic structures in momentum space, while its emergence from real-space processes in strongly interacting systems remains largely unexplored. Here, we study a doped charge-transfer insulator in a strongly repulsive spinless-fermion model with three sublattices and $2π$ flux per unit cell. Combining perturbative analysis, exact diagonalization, and density matrix renormalization group simulations, we establish a topological superconducting ground state with $p+ip$ symmetry. In the large charge-transfer gap limit, chiral charge-transfer excitations generate a correlated-hopping process that provides a microscopic mechanism for electron pairing and its chiral structure. The chiral superconductivity persists into the smaller-gap regime, where chiral excitonic two-particle bound state can emerge. Our results establish a concrete real-space route to topological chiral superconductivity upon doping strongly interacting charge-transfer insulators with orbital magnetism.

items.title: Asymmetric $q$-Gaussian Distributions from Tsallis Maximum Entropy
items.summary: Within the framework of non-extensive statistical mechanics, $q$-Gaussian distributions arise as maximum-entropy solutions of Tsallis entropy under suitable escort moment constraints. Although widely used in physics, biology, geology, finance, and related fields, standard $q$-Gaussians are intrinsically symmetric and cannot capture asymmetric fluctuations often observed in empirical data. We ask whether asymmetry can arise from the Tsallis maximum-entropy principle without externally skewing or joining distributions. We show that this is achieved by retaining the Tsallis entropy and imposing a global escort mean together with distinct downside and upside escort semi-variances. The key step is to reformulate the problem of maximum Tsallis entropy in terms of the escort density. The nonlinear escort constraints then become affine, while maximizing Tsallis entropy becomes equivalent to maximizing a strictly concave functional over a convex feasible set. Consequently, any admissible stationary solution is the unique global maximizer of the corresponding variational problem. The finite-sample approximation properties of the proposed asymmetric $q$-Gaussian are studied through Monte Carlo experiments using synthetic data generated from Azzalini skew-Student distributions. Compared with the classical symmetric $q$-Gaussian, the asymmetric specification systematically provides a closer approximation to synthetic asymmetric heavy-tailed distributions. Finally, we fit the model to return series from major equity indices, a commodity, and cryptocurrencies, and compare its in-sample goodness of fit with that of a symmetric $q$-Gaussian. The results show that the asymmetric model offers a closer in-sample description of unconditional return distributions, most clearly in the tails.

items.title: Nontrivial topological properties from the cooperation of static perturbations and Floquet fields in type-II semi-Dirac semimetals
items.summary: In this work, we present a comprehensive theoretical study for the topological and anomalous transport properties of type-II SDSMs under three scenarios, i.e., static symmetry-breaking perturbations, periodic Floquet driving by two-frequency orthogonally polarized light (TFOPL), and their cooperative effects in the hybrid scenario. We first show that a static mass $m_z$ opens a bulk gap and drives the system into a Chern insulator with Chern number $C^{\rm per}=\pm 2\,{\rm sgn}(m_z)$. In comparison, TFOPL alone only shifts the positions of Dirac points and cannot open a full gap. Nevertheless, it produces a Berry curvature odd in the $x$-direction, yielding a finite Berry curvature dipole (BCD) along $x$ proportional to the sine of the initial phase, while the $y$-component vanishes. The hybrid scenario, by contrast, exhibits a remarkably rich phenomenology. Specifically, its gap-closure criterion becomes cubic and thus admits up to three real roots when the effective parameter along the $x$-direction is negative, thereby producing multiple light-tunable gap-closing points and a series of topological phase transitions. In particular, the BCD exhibits a double-peak structure with strong enhancement near gap-closing manifolds and synchronized sign reversal of the full vector under external tuning. We further analyze the anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC), anomalous Nernst conductivity (ANC), and anomalous thermal Hall conductivity (ATHC). The AHC and ATHC exhibit quantized plateaus that serve as signatures of Chern-insulator phases, while the ANC, being a Fermi-surface probe, provides complementary local information and can identify light-induced gaps even when global topological invariants remain unchanged. Taken together, these results offer useful insights into the topological properties of 2D type-II SDSMs and related systems.

items.title: Solubility of poorly soluble species in bulk and nanopores from grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling
items.summary: Poorly soluble species can have mean populations below one in small systems such as nanopores. In this regime, the grand-potential minimum, which identifies the most probable particle number, differs from the ensemble-averaged solute loading. We use grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling (GCWLS) to calculate the density of states $Ω(N_\mathrm{A}, N_\mathrm{B})$ for a binary Lennard-Jones mixture of solute B in solvent A, both in bulk and in slit pores. One set of GCWLS simulations gives ensemble averages over a range of chemical potentials, whereas conventional grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation requires a separate simulation at each state point. Independent GCMC simulations confirm the GCWLS ensemble averages. The solvent number distribution is nearly Gaussian, whereas the dilute solute distribution is skewed and Poisson-like. The most probable solute number therefore lies below the ensemble-averaged loading $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle$ and is zero whenever $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle<1$. Reading the solute loading from the grand-potential minimum underestimates it and can falsely indicate that no solute is present. Defining the oversolubility as $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}=x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{conf}}/x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{bulk}}$, where $x_\mathrm{B}$ is the solute mole fraction, we find $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}\approx12$ in a pore of 3.5 particle diameters width when both wall interactions are repulsive. Adding wall-solute attraction moderately raises it to $\approx13$, whereas wall-solvent attraction lowers it to $\approx3.4$. This comparison shows that the wall-solvent interaction controls most of the enhancement. As the pore widens, $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}$ decreases toward unity. In bulk and in nanopores alike, the solubility of poorly soluble species should be obtained from ensemble averages rather than from grand-potential minima.

items.title: Observation of a Novel Charge Density Wave Superstructure in Monolayer 1T-$VS_{2}$ at Room Temperature and its Evolution in Multilayers
items.summary: Spontaneous formation of charge density wave (CDW) superstructures in monolayers (MLs) of a two-dimensional (2D) crystal lattice is fundamental in understanding its complex quantum states. We report a successful top-down liquid phase exfoliation and stamp transfer process (LPESTP) to create ML VS\textsubscript{2}, undergoing a CDW transition at room temperature. Using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and electron diffraction (ED), we observed the coexistence of 1T and 2H polymorphic phases in VS\textsubscript{2} at room temperature, and only the 1T phase undergoes CDW transition. We discovered a novel incommensurate CDW superstructure ($\sqrt{7} \times \sqrt{7}$) R19.1\textsuperscript{o} in ML 1T-VS\textsubscript{2}. With an increase in the number of layers, the CDW order changes to a commensurate ($2 \times 2\times 1$) superstructure. Using angle-dependent photoelectron spectroscopy and TEM, we have shown that vanadium atoms self-intercalate as V\textsuperscript{3+} ions in multilayer VS\textsubscript{2} and are responsible for the evolution of the CDW superstructure from the incommensurate ($\sqrt{7} \times \sqrt{7}$) R 19.1\textsuperscript{o} to the commensurate ($2\times2\times1$) order. We also report the observation of novel Moiré superlattices in twisted bilayer 1T-VS\textsubscript{2} flakes with trapped CDW superstructure of the monolayer. The density functional theory (DFT) calculation performed on ML 1T-VS\textsubscript{2} show that the observed ($\sqrt{7} \times \sqrt{7}$) R 19.1\textsuperscript{o} CDW superstructure has lower energy compared to that of the pristine undistorted ML and the CDW instability is driven by formation of strong soft-phonon modes. Our findings provide an important platform for understanding the evolution of CDW superstructures in 1T-VS\textsubscript{2} with layer numbers and V self-intercalation.

items.title: Admittance extraction of quantum dot arrays for charge sensing
items.summary: This work demonstrates admittance extraction of quantum dot arrays using a rate equation frame- work matching experimental reflectometry measurements. Using a semiclassical rate equation, we consider a perturbation of the source/drain chemical potential to model reflectometry readout in a quantum dot array. This is a time-dependent extension of the rate equation which has been employed in literature for pumped arrays of quantum dots and capacitance extractions. Here we extend this to a double quantum dot for admittance extraction. The simulations are calibrated us- ing Fermi-Hubbard parameters extracted from experimental data, which it is then shown to closely approximate to.

items.title: Tailored VxOy Metal--Insulator-Transition Oxides for Temperature-Triggered Smart Insulation in Superconducting Coils
items.summary: Smart insulation is a turn-to-turn layer that insulates in normal operation and conducts only near a hot spot. It could combine the fast ramping of insulated coils with the passive energy dump of non-insulated coils. Metal-insulator transition (MIT) oxides are natural candidates, but the only one tested in a coil so far, V2O3, switches at 150-170 K, far above the 30-70 K window useful for REBCO magnets. We explore the vanadium-oxygen system to lower the transition. TGA redox processing produced multi-phase powders with an effective transition near 127 K, about 25 K below V2O3. Hydrothermal V3O7, hydrated or annealed, was far too resistive and showed no usable transition. V2O3-epoxy specimens provided a robust reference and an acceptance criterion. Cryogenic measurements revealed a reproducible thermal hysteresis, and the measured specific heat of V2O3 corrects earlier model inputs by close to two orders of magnitude. A first electro-thermal model reproduces current sharing through the smart-insulation layer. Doped V2O3 and V8O15 are identified as the next targets.

items.title: Preconditioning Magnetic Systems in Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory
items.summary: The convergence of the self-consistent field iterations in Kohn-Sham density functional theory can be significantly hindered by the presence of small eigenvalues in the dielectric matrix, which are often associated with electronic phase transitions in magnetic systems. In this work, we study this type of convergence issues and propose a new preconditioning scheme to mitigate them. Our preconditioning scheme is inspired by the Stoner model and based on a non-interacting susceptibility that neglects orbital variations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a range of ferromagnetic systems, showing that it can significantly reduce the number of iterations required to achieve convergence in the vicinity of magnetic phase transitions.

items.title: Locally optimized variational evolution for quantum many-body systems
items.summary: Quantum many-body dynamics is difficult to simulate because the global wavefunction develops extensive complexity, whereas local observables may retain only an intrinsic, system-size-independent complexity. This distinction is especially relevant in thermalizing systems, where local subsystems lose microscopic information and relax towards equilibrium. We introduce a variational time-evolution principle that exploits this separation by replacing global-state fidelity with a cost function defined on local reduced density matrices. The resulting locally optimized matrix-product-state (LOMPS) algorithm retains coherent short-time dynamics while using the simplification generated by thermalization at later times, and admits closed-form equations of motion analogous to the time-dependent variational principle. The same principle yields a quantum-classical algorithm in which a quantum processor evaluates the local cost and a noise-robust classical procedure performs the optimization. Proof-of-principle implementations on Quantinuum H2 and IBM Heron processors recover the characteristic local dynamics.

items.title: Probing quantum nonlinear phononics in multilayer graphene with time-resolved Raman scattering
items.summary: Coherently driven phonons are conventionally described classically. Nonlinear phonon-phonon interactions, however, allow an infrared drive to reshape the fluctuation spectrum and generate substantial nonthermal enhancement of phonon fluctuations, motivating a description beyond the coherent displacement alone. We benchmark classical and semiclassical approximations against the full quantum theory and find that the semiclassical treatment substantially improves agreement with the quantum dynamics. We propose nonequilibrium spontaneous Raman scattering as a sensitive probe of these effects and apply our framework to recent experiments suggesting quantum nonlinear phononics involving the $\mathrm{E}_{1u}$ and $\mathrm{E}_{2g}$ modes in multilayer graphene. At very strong pump fields, driving the $\mathrm{E}_{1u}$ mode significantly modifies the $\mathrm{E}_{2g}$ Raman spectrum; however, reproducing the reported response at experimental field strengths requires accounting for pump-induced Raman matrix element dynamics or alternative energy pathways into the $\mathrm{E}_{2g}$ mode. Our findings extend nonlinear phononics beyond average atomic displacements to the dynamics of lattice fluctuations, highlighting the interplay between coherent motion and quantum correlations in driven materials.

items.title: PDEformer-2: a versatile foundation model for two-dimensional partial differential equations
items.summary: Abstract Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental to modeling physical systems. Traditional PDE solvers are often computationally expensive. Neural operators require independent training for different PDEs, and tend to be data-greedy when adapted to new scenarios. To this end, we introduce PDEformer-2, a versatile foundation model for solving diverse two-dimensional PDEs. The model receives the PDE form as input through a flexible computational graph representation and outputs solutions that can be queried at any spatio-temporal point. Pretrained on a 40 TB dataset spanning varied equation types, domains, boundary conditions, variable counts, and time dependence, PDEformer-2 enables instant zero-shot predictions for familiar PDEs and adapts faster to unseen ones than specialized baselines, achieving lower errors with limited samples. It also facilitates efficient inverse problem solving, successfully recovering unknown PDE parameters, including scalar coefficients and fields, in experiments.

items.title: Air-gap engineering enabled ultrafast 9-bit ferroelectric semi-gate transistor array for high-efficiency image denoising
items.summary: Abstract The insufficient lateral electric field gradient limits the programming/erasing speed of conventional semi-floating gate transistors, while charge leakage leads to poor data retention and compromised operating characteristics. Here we design a ferroelectric semi-gate (FSG) transistor featuring a triangular air gap adjacent to the drain region. The device exhibits an as-programmed on–off ratio exceeding 10 7 , remaining above 10 5 after 11 weeks, and a memory window of approximately 6 V. The localized lateral electric field accelerates program and erase operations to 60 ns and 75 ns, respectively. The spontaneous polarization field of the ferroelectric HfZrO layer strengthens charge retention in the HfO 2 charge-trapping layer, enabling robust nonvolatile memory performance with a retention time exceeding 10 6 s. This synergistic integration of air-gap engineering and ferroelectric polarization yields an optimal trade-off between speed, retention and multilevel operation. By exploiting its superior multilevel capability with 9-bit distinguishable current states, we realize Ising-model-based image denoising using a 32 × 32 transistor array. These FSG transistors show promising potential for high-speed, low-power random-access memory applications.

items.title: Quantal PCR: A Calibrator-Free Method for Determining the Unit for Nucleic Acid Quantification
Global hotspots and trends of ecological water scarcity in river basins
items.summary: Abstract Healthy freshwater ecosystems are crucial for sustainable development, yet they face growing threats from unsustainable water use. However, current water scarcity metrics focus almost exclusively on human demand, overlooking whether sufficient water remains to sustain ecosystems. We address this gap by presenting the first evaluation of ecological water scarcity (EWS) across 1,182 river basins, introducing a novel indicator that recognizes ecosystems as legitimate water users to those of humans. Our findings reveal that in the 2000s, 412 basins (35% globally; 17% annual, 18% seasonal) experienced EWS, with affected areas expanding by 10 million km² since the 1950s. Human intervention intensified EWS in 13% of basins and caused 53% of seasonal and 60% of annual EWS cases. By the 2050s, affected basins range from 392 under RCP2.6–SSP1 to 416 under RCP8.5–SSP5, with persistent hotspots in regions of intensive water use. These findings show that climate mitigation can reduce future EWS risk, but environmental flow protection, water-use efficiency, water recycling, ecologically informed infrastructure operation and ecosystem restoration are also needed to safeguard freshwater ecosystems.

authors: G. W. Collins, S. Seager, J. Eggert, X. Gong, M. Huff, J. R. Rygg, T.-A. Suer, and R. Jeanloz
items.summary: W. Collins, S. Seager, J. Eggert, X. Gong, M. Huff, J. R. Rygg, T.-A. Suer, and R. Jeanloz Astronomers observe thousands of planets beyond our Solar System, many with extreme interior conditions. Deep inside these worlds, gravity produces pressures millions to billions of times stronger than Earth’s atmosphere. At these pressures, matter behaves in surprising ways: hydrogen can become metallic, water and ammonia may form exotic superionic states, and hydrocarbons can turn into diamond. This Colloquium describes how studying these unusual materials helps scientists explain how planets form, evolve, and generate magnetic fields and magma oceans. Using powerful lasers and pulsed-power facilities, researchers recreate such pressures in laboratories, revealing new physics and improving understanding of the hidden interiors of distant planets.
